title: Sarah Ferguson expected back in the UK shortly, source tells BBC
description: Ferguson is expected to move into the six-bedroom home "imminently", which could be as soon as next week, the Sun reported, external.It is believed sh
body: Ferguson is expected to move into the six-bedroom home "imminently", which could be as soon as next week, the Sun reported, external.It is believed she has been spending her time out of the public eye at an Alpine chalet in Verbier, Switzerland, since leaving Royal Lodge. Her belongings were collected from Mountbatten-Windsor's home in Sandringham this week, the newspaper added.She had been keeping a low profile since losing her titles alongside Mountbatten-Windsor after she became mired in the scandal about her connections to Epstein, and faced calls to speak to US authorities after last year's release of millions of documents shed new light on their relationship.In one email exchange from 2011, she appeared to privately apologise for her public rejection of Epstein, saying: "You have always been a steadfast, generous and supreme friend to me and my family." A spokesperson for the duchess previously said the email was sent after Epstein had threatened to sue her for defamation - in an effort to convince him not to.Another email suggested Ferguson took her daughters to see Epstein in the US days after he was released from prison for child sex crimes.The emails do not indicate any wrongdoing.Epstein was also ultimately the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of "serious lapses of judgment" over his friendship with the late paedophile. Mountbatten-Windsor has always denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.Ferguson lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and reverted to her maiden name, and also lost the freedom of the city of York after councillors voted unanimously to remove the honour over the scandal.Her expected return comes just days after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex came back to Britain with their children to begin a new life after six years living in the US.

schema.headline: Sarah Ferguson expected back in the UK shortly, source tells BBC

title: Norway's Haakon remembers 'my dear father' in first speech as king
description: Haakon stressed national unity in the speech, saying the royal family believed in a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal valu
body: Haakon stressed national unity in the speech, saying the royal family believed in a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value".    He said Harald had been a good father to himself and his sister, Princess Märtha Louise, as well as a "warm and funny grandfather" to his six grandchildren and a "loving and caring husband" to his widow, Queen Sonja.The new king appeared to choke back tears as he noted that Saturday would have been their 58th wedding anniversary.Harald brought the family together "with a natural authority", of which he might not have been aware himself, his son recalled.He had "always stayed true" to his "values and commitments", the new king stressed."He constantly reminded us in the family that each of us must do things in our own way. Find our own style. Be ourselves," Haakon said.He also remarked on the "powerful and moving experience" of seeing thousands of Norwegians gather outside the royal palace in the capital Oslo with "flowers, tributes and candles"."We are in mourning, yet at the same time it brings comfort and strength that so many are grieving together with us," he said.Norwegians have been laying flowers outside the royal palace in Oslo since news broke that Harald had died on Friday. A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet given for his funeral.Among them was Norway's Prime Minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service with his wife, Queen Mette-Marit - a stripped-down version of a coronation, which Norway no longer holds.He assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.Mette-Marit came under scrutiny when it was revealed that she had had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised.She later received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when Haakon married his mother.Haakon's sister, Märtha Louise, has also courted controversy for remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024, their business activities ultimately leading her to step back from royal duties.Without directly referencing these controversies, Haakon said during his speech: "Our family has experienced the importance of standing together in order to remain steadfast both within ourselves and for one another even during difficult times."He said he, along with Mette-Marit and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, would "always strive to understand the life situations of different people".He added: "No one who lives in this country knows what we will face together, but what we do know is that we will stand by one another through both good days and difficult ones."Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year suggested that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

schema.headline: Norway's Haakon remembers 'my dear father' in first speech as king

title: Tibet-Nepal floods: Shocking footage isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
description: On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launc
body: On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled. Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it. It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents. The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long. Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.

schema.headline: Tibet-Nepal floods: Shocking footage isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there

title: Croatian refugee tracks down Mold siblings who sent him a gift 33 years ago
description: A man forced to flee war in Croatia as a child has used social media to find and thank the siblings from Wales, who sent him a Christmas present more
body: A man forced to flee war in Croatia as a child has used social media to find and thank the siblings from Wales, who sent him a Christmas present more than 30 years ago.Dalibor Sentic was 10 when in the early 1990s his family fled the newly independent country - which had recently become involved in the Balkan war - for Stockholm, Sweden.Dalibor had received a gift from two young siblings, eight-year-old Claire and Peter, six, from Mold, Flintshire, and had hoped to track them down but only had limited information on them.Decades later, Dalibor, now 44, was able to find the pair to thank them, saying the gesture had "meant a lot" at a time of great difficulty.Describing fleeing his homeland as a child, Dalibor said "we had basically nothing"."It was like starting all over again."I was so innocent but remember hearing the bombs," he said.Dalibor said that, despite the conflict surrounding them, his parents made sure he felt "loved and secure", although he added that moving countries was "tough on a kid". Some months before they fled, Dalibor said his teacher took him into a room full of packages, telling him to choose one to open.It contained a picture of Claire and Peter, which he held onto for more than three decades. "The older you get the more you understand the meaning behind small gestures... it meant a lot," he said.

schema.headline: Croatian refugee tracks down Mold siblings who sent him a gift 33 years ago

title: Serious questions over use of UK emergency alerts, its creators say
description: As the Conservative minister who launched the UK's emergency alert system, Oliver Dowden was more than familiar with the loud bleeping sound coming fr
body: As the Conservative minister who launched the UK's emergency alert system, Oliver Dowden was more than familiar with the loud bleeping sound coming from his phone earlier this month.What took him by a surprise was the message on the screen.Like millions of people across England and Wales, the "severe alert" on 14 August warned him of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" and against doing anything that could start a fire, including lighting disposable barbecues.It was the biggest use of the system to date - but Dowden has now weighed in to question whether it was strictly necessary.Dowden and two officials who helped create the government's emergency alert system are calling for Labour ministers to be up front with the public on what it could be used for in future."I was surprised at the decision to issue this nationwide alert and it raises some serious questions," Dowden, who served as deputy prime minister under Rishi Sunak, tells BBC News."The government needs to clarify the criteria for its use and why this alert met those criteria."The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August.It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk, and confusion about alerts sent multiple times.Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales."People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it."A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts."Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds.The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries."By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said.But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring.He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around."Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'."His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?"Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life."It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out.Back in 2021 when designing the alerts, he says these were the scenarios considered valid for future alerts:PandemicsSevere weather and environmental alerts such as flood riskCounter-terrorismBomb disposal evacuationMajor hazards such as the Buncefield oil depot fire in 2005WildfiresCoal tip landslidesWhen building the UK alert system, which cost up to £25.3m in its first three years, officials looked to Australia, external and New Zealand, external where emergency alerts have no "opt out" option for the public, unlike in the UK. They also considered minor types of public safety alerts which are sent in the US for issues such as missing children.The alert targets individual cell towers with a radiowave-like signal, allowing all mobile phones in the area to pick it up without needing to know people's mobile numbers. This cell broadcast technology is used instead of SMS texts or an app.It comes as the Cabinet Office plans to launch a separate campaign in the autumn about how people can make themselves and their homes more prepared for extreme weather and cyber-attacks.Another one of those involved in creating the alert system, Nick Corney, thinks the government "missed a trick" with the wildfire alert by sending it nationally rather than targeted at specific postcodes with the highest risk.Corney, who worked in the Cabinet Office between 2018 and 2021 and says he was in weekly and then daily meetings about designing alerts, wants a "thorough review".He says this would look at making future alert wording more specific, such as explaining the threat to life with a link to a webpage. "An extra level of consideration needs to be put in place" for national alert versus a local one, he adds."You've really got to take yourself out of the Cobra room," he says."There's a level of scaring the public that needs to be taken into consideration."

schema.headline: Serious questions over use of UK emergency alerts, its creators say

title: Cody Gakpo transfer news: Manchester City open talks with Liverpool
description: Liverpool view Gakpo as a proven multi-functional Premier League attacker and he has shown that with a goal and an assist in their first two games thi
body: Liverpool view Gakpo as a proven multi-functional Premier League attacker and he has shown that with a goal and an assist in their first two games this season.But all summer, the understanding has been that if the club bring in the attacking players they want, they would not stand in the way of Gakpo if a solid offer came in. Given how late in the transfer window the talks are taking place between Liverpool and Manchester City, the Anfield side will now consider the situation before sanctioning any move. Liverpool are also hoping to bring in another winger before deadline day.With the arrival of Victor Munoz, the emergence of Rio Ngumoha and Barcola's imminent move from PSG, Gakpo is well aware that he may not be first choice any more, so if a move does happen it would not come as a surprise.Financially it will be a great outcome for Liverpool if they agree a deal for about £85m given they signed Gakpo for £35m from PSV Eindhoven after the World Cup in 2022.But with Hugo Ekitike missing until 2027 with a ruptured Achilles tendon, and Isak's injury struggles, they would be taking a massive risk letting Gakpo leave.

title: 'Keep walking, keep happy': 100-year-old still does a mile a day
description: Image caption, Centenarian Peter Byers enjoys walking and regular fishing tripsByEast Yorkshire and Lincolnshire health and social care correspondentF
body: Image caption, Centenarian Peter Byers enjoys walking and regular fishing tripsByEast Yorkshire and Lincolnshire health and social care correspondentFor 100-year-old Peter Byers, the secret to a long, active life is to "keep happy, keep walking and "keep breathing".The father of five from Pocklington, East Yorkshire, said he walked into town most days "to make sure people know I'm still alive."Peter, who underwent heart surgery five years ago, also enjoys week-long fishing breaks with his son.He said his mobility scooter was gathering dust in the garage, adding: "I go and charge it up regularly like I'm supposed to, but it's never moved."Image source, Family photoImage caption, Peter Byers with his 100th birthday card from the KingPeter said walking helped him "escape the four walls", meet people and, most importantly, "keep my legs going".Five years ago, he had heart surgery at Castle Hill Hospital, near Hull, to treat severe aortic stenosis."It was all explained to me what they were going to do. It's an iffy thing, but I said 'go for it'. And it's done me the world of good."It perked me up. I started to enjoy life again. I started back on American Square dancing and I go out with my children. We do everything together."Asked what his family think of his new lease of life, he laughed and said: "They think I'm a nuisance. I'm keeping saying, 'let's do this, let's do that'."Image source, Family photoImage caption, Peter Byers travelled the world with the Royal Corps of SignalsA patient's age does not need to be a barrier to treatment, according to the cardiology team at Castle Hill.Dr Manish Ramlall, a consultant intervention cardiologist, said: "Mr Byers is a very well man, leading a very active life, and, for him, age is very much just a number."Peter served in the Royal Navy and the Royal Corps of Signals, a career that took him round the world and allowed him to enjoy his passion for fishing as far afield as Malaysia."It's a good life, and you've got to make the best of it," he said. "Keep happy, keep walking."He said he received a card for his 90th birthday that set out the secret to a long and active life."It said 'keep breathing', which I thought was a good idea."

schema.headline: 'Keep walking, keep happy': 100-year-old still does a mile a day

title: Esports: How to get £2,000 to play computer games at university
description: Dray encouraged students to make use of every scholarship, bursary and opportunity available to them.He said: "Many of these funds are available to mo
body: Dray encouraged students to make use of every scholarship, bursary and opportunity available to them.He said: "Many of these funds are available to more students than they realise, and everyone should be taking full advantage."The average graduate in England leaves university with debts of more than £47,500. Scholarships such as Roehampton's can reduce student debt and provide additional financial support.Thomas Cole, an esports player nicknamed Pac who specialises in the racing game Trackmania, said universities offering unique scholarships, including esports, encourages students academically by reducing the level of financial stress they might face.  "Uni students being paid to play a game alongside doing their studies, it's definitely cracking. If I had gone to uni, I would have loved that," he says."If it doesn't let the academic side suffer, then I think being offered something like that really spurs on people to be better in gaming," he says.Tom Allingham, student money expert from the Save the Student personal finance site, regularly advises incoming first years to seek out scholarships and learn more about what their university offers. "Unfortunately, I don't think there is enough awareness on scholarships," he said. "There is a lot of funding that goes unclaimed because students don't know that they're eligible for it," he added.Save the Student helps share various scholarships and bursaries on their website. "What we try to get across is you can get extra funding for so many different reasons."

schema.headline: Esports: How to get £2,000 to play computer games at university

title: Burnham's summer tour is over - now he has to prove himself in Parliament
description: Andy Burnham is set to come under the most intense scrutiny of his political life when Parliament returns on Tuesday.Since coming to power six weeks a
body: Andy Burnham is set to come under the most intense scrutiny of his political life when Parliament returns on Tuesday.Since coming to power six weeks ago, the new prime minister has largely been free to set his own agenda.The timing of Labour's leadership contest meant he walked into Number 10 after the House of Commons began its summer break, denying MPs the chance to question him and creating what some have seen as a honeymoon period. Burnham has embarked on what Downing Street called a "summer tour" of the UK, appeared on podcasts and announced a series of eye-catching policies, mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.But things are about to get a lot tougher, with MPs finally getting a chance to grill the new PM when he makes a statement to Parliament on his priorities as PM.He has taken questions from MPs in the Commons before, when he was a minister in Tony Blair and Gordon Brown's Labour governments.But Tuesday will be his first appearance on the government front bench for 16 years.The team around Burnham view the start of his premiership as successful but say they will be relieved to get back to the "structure" of parliamentary politics.Burnham will know he has really arrived as PM when he makes his debut at prime minister's questions (PMQs) on Wednesday, after almost two decades of trying to get there.A packed Commons chamber, with curveball questions, hostile opposition politicians and the biggest TV and online audience of the week will be a world away from his nine years as Mayor of Greater Manchester.One Number 10 source said Burnham's debut would be used as a "learning exercise" to discover "what works and what doesn't".The new PM is said to be keen to adopt a "tonal shift" at the weekly half-hour session and will attempt to bring more humour to the occasion.Most prime ministers enter PMQs with a thick folder of notes covering what they hope is every conceivable question they might face.Burnham likes to speak without notes, as he did in his first speech outside Downing Street, and is thought to be considering doing the same at PMQs.His aides sound equally relaxed about the task ahead, even though the next few weeks could define his entire premiership.Message discipline is being emphasised inside the Treasury too.The biggest moment for the Burnham government this autumn will come on 28 October, when Chancellor John Healey unveils the Budget.Sir Keir and his chancellor Rachel Reeves were widely seen to have been damaged politically when many of the policies in their Budgets made their way into the media.In response, Burnham's administration has put measures in place to try to stop those leaks and it's understood the Treasury is telling officials that Budget security is like national security.Nevertheless, speculation about the Budget is likely to dominate the coming weeks in Westminster, in particular questions about what taxes could potentially be increased.Burnham has repeatedly said he will keep Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance.But the prime minister has also said there is "room for movement" on taxes within that pledge, leading the Conservatives to believe it's a fruitful topic for political attacks.The Treasury is focused on creating a Budget that will not spook financial markets, with a senior source insisting the core themes of Healey's plans would be "fiscal discipline" and "fiscal devolution".Healey resigned as Sir Keir's defence secretary over what he saw as a failure to adequately fund the armed forces.It now falls to him to find the money to fund the defence investment plan, with an extra £4.7bn needed in the Budget.Healey is not expected to set out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence in the Budget, and will instead wait until next spring's Spending Review.When asked if there was nervousness about potentially annoying military chiefs, a senior Treasury source said you'd be "hard-placed to find anyone sceptical" of the idea that Healey is committed to keeping the country safe.There has also been speculation that Burnham wants to weaken the Treasury's traditionally tight grip on policies across government.Just before Parliament broke up for summer, the government said it was transferring "local economic growth policy" from the Treasury to Burnham's new Manchester base Number 10 North.The Treasury is downplaying the idea that Number 10 North could become in effect a rival department.Despite predominantly focusing on domestic issues so far, Burnham will also turn his attention to foreign policy, with a visit to Downing Street by French President Emmanuel Macron.And, finally, he will need to make sure he keeps his own troops in Parliament happier than they were under the previous management.Many Labour backbenchers felt that Sir Keir did not listen to them enough and Burnham is expected to be far more visible in the Commons voting lobbies and tea rooms than his predecessor.Sources say he met most Labour MPs in the weeks before he became prime minister and believes that MPs "value that bit of face time".But there is still a divide among the more than 400 Labour MPs about what policy areas should be prioritised at a time when the financial situation looks set to be tricky for some time.Those around the prime minister are conscious, too, of the difficult decisions that may lie ahead.One Number 10 source said there was an acknowledgement in Downing Street that the "public's expectation bar is high and we've got to meet it".

schema.headline: Burnham's summer tour is over - now he has to prove himself in Parliament

title: Spurs 0-2 Newcastle: Magpies show there's plenty of life after Tonali
description: Sandro Tonali anticipated being "more nervous" than usual about coming up against former club Newcastle United for the first time.You suspect the Tott
body: Sandro Tonali anticipated being "more nervous" than usual about coming up against former club Newcastle United for the first time.You suspect the Tottenham Hotspur midfielder felt a little sick following their 2-0 defeat on Saturday evening."Sandro, what's the score?" the away fans taunted in the closing stages as the substituted Italian looked on.This bruising loss was certainly not the reunion Tonali had in mind after joining Spurs for a fee worth up to £100m last month.It is still very early days, of course, but Newcastle appear to have reinvested the money wisely after spending a similar combined amount on midfielder Nico Gonzalez, defender Amar Dedic and goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek.A number of the players head coach Matthias Jaissle inherited, such as goalscorers Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa, also look reborn.Yet he was rightly not getting carried away following his first Premier League win."We have our own goals and we are clear with that," Jaissle said. "We are also realistic. Now you write everything is top, everything is great. "We don't follow that too much. We are emotionally very stable and don't see the highs higher than it is now. "It is a moment to enjoy as well after that start, but we are also smart enough to see a long journey ahead of us and there will be challenges as well."Jaissle, by his own admission, "likes challenges" and this was certainly a big one to take on.It is exactly 30 days since predecessor Eddie Howe oversaw what proved to be his final match in charge, a sobering 4-1 friendly defeat against Bristol City, before stepping down.Newcastle had sold Tonali. Anthony Gordon had left for Barcelona. Captain Bruno Guimaraes' sights were set on a move to Arsenal.The start of the season was also rapidly approaching.Newcastle have made further additions since then, but only one of their seven summer signings, Gonzalez, has previously played in the Premier League.All of the new arrivals are aged 24 and under.Yet you would not necessarily know it by the immediate impact full-back Dedic has made following his £30m move from Benfica, or how Hornicek has stood up to the physicality of the Premier League since his £25.7m switch from Braga.It could easily be forgotten, given what happened after the break at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, but Hornicek was among those to play an important role in this win after making three saves at crucial moments in the first half.No wonder Jaissle clenched his fists on the touchline after Hornicek got a strong hand behind Jan Paul van Hecke's header. There was a similarly enthusiastic reaction from the former Hoffenheim defender when Lewis Hall blocked a goalbound effort from Pedro Porro in the first half."In the first half, we didn't play a really good game, but we could really count on everyone throwing everything into every ball and every cross," Jaissle said. "This is the commitment and belief that we can keep the clean sheet, so that makes me proud."Although Newcastle defeated Spurs last season, too, there were also a number of games when the visitors wilted in such circumstances.Newcastle won just four of their 19 top-flight matches on the road and, home or away, they had not previously kept a single clean sheet since March.However, going in level in their first away day of this campaign gave Newcastle the chance to regroup at half-time.The visitors sought to be more aggressive after the break and clinically took Spurs apart with their only two shots on target.For the first, just as he did in the opening stages, new signing Gonzalez hit a stunning cross field ball over the head of Spurs left-back Andy Robertson for the advancing Dedic to flick on to Elanga, who turned Tonali inside the box and fired the ball in off the post."It is something that I spoke about with the coach, even before the game," Gonzalez said. "He wanted me to see these kind of balls and I tried a few in the first half and the second half, and we scored."In the second half we said, 'we have to keep doing this' because it is really hard to defend players like Amar, a full-back that comes this fast from behind. Normally wingers don't defend these kind of balls very well."It's something that we have to keep doing and I hope it gives us many more goals this season."For Newcastle's second, Sean Steur's corner was headed down by fellow substitute Nick Woltemade and Wissa improvised with a clever overhead kick to double his side's lead.For all the focus on Newcastle's new arrivals, it was rather fitting that two players who endured difficult first seasons at the club stepped up under Jaissle once again as Elanga and Wissa built on improved showings against Liverpool on the opening weekend."He's a really dynamic manager so we need to give everything," Wissa told Sky Sports. "I think he's the best signing."

schema.headline: Spurs 0-2 Newcastle: Magpies show there's plenty of life after Tonali

title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
description: Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.The brother of
body: Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister."Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region. The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of £5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts. And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.Tiwari, 51, had travelled to Nepal to take part in the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra pilgrimage, which was "her dream", her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC.She travelled to Delhi from London before heading to Kathmandu on 14 August with a group from the spiritual organisation Isha Foundation.Tiwari was expected to return to India on Thursday and meet her brother and parents. But now, the family is desperately searching for answers."We have called every helpline given by the Indian government and reached out to the British Embassy in Kathmandu as well," Goyal said."Please help us find her," he said, his voice breaking. "We are all very scared."Neetu's husband, Shantanu, added she had been at the Gyirong checkpoint when the floods struck, so the search for her is being coordinated by China. Anant Patel told BBC Your Voice that he is still waiting for news on his missing parents, Bipin and Mala Patel, who are from Coventry. The 29-year-old believes his parents - who are also on a pilgrimage - crossed into Tibet from Nepal moments before the landslide hit the Gyirong border crossing.He and his brother Deepesh are in touch with the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, and he told the BBC: "It's a difficult situation for us all, and we are doing our best to stay strong as best as we can in the circumstances."Pramod Poudel, who lives in Uckfield in East Sussex, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife Sumitra Sapkota and family since the flood hit on Wednesday."It's a very, very difficult time for me and for my family and my country at this moment, but obviously I have to go and see what's happening there," he said.Poudel, who goes by the name Pedro, said he is travelling home to Nepal because "my family needs me".The daughter of Hemangini Patel, 65, said she is still yet to hear from her mother or her aunt Hema Amin, 63.Patel told BBC Your Voice her mother's last known location is from a TikTok video shared at 06:00 Nepal time, crossing into Tibet.She said her mother and aunt had been travelling with the Alpine Eco Trek tour when the flooding hit."We are trying to get through to British embassy in China but can't even get through," Patel said.Essex nurse Rajendra Pudasaini said his relatives were "swept away" by the floods."My wife's auntie and uncle, and their granddaughter and her husband are missing, and my godson as well," he said. "They're gone. The speed the water came, they couldn't be saved, they were just swept away."Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he hasn't heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, and sister-in-law Ankita Chandra, 35.He said he'd last heard from Ankit on 26 August when he had been travelling with tour operator Kailash Journey on a pilgrimage.The whole group is now missing, Ranjan said, adding: "We don't know if they crossed the border... We don't have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated." Also missing is Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse at Darent Valley Hospital in Kent. Her brother Shambhu said that her family was desperately waiting for news of her safety after she lost contact with her relatives while on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash. "My dear sister, wherever you are, please stay strong. We are praying for your safety every moment and waiting desperately for you to return home," he wrote on social media.A family of four, including an 18-year-old A-Level student and a 13-year-old girl, from Surrey are also among the missing. Spandan Sahu, 18, was in Nepal with his father Santosh Sahu, 46, his mother Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44, and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.Spandan had just finished his A-levels at Royal Grammar School Guildford.In a statement, a spokesperson for the school said: "It is with great concern that we have been informed that a former student, along with members of his family, have been reported missing in Nepal."Whilst we are hoping for positive news, we do not have any further information at this time."Our thoughts, love and deepest sympathies are with all of the families and loved ones of anyone affected by this tragedy in Nepal at this incredibly difficult time."Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy, since the flooding hit. Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit. "We're not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week," Kolagatla added."The kids still don't believe it. They think she's stuck in the flood and that she'll come back. They think she's stuck somewhere and there's no mobile network."Prajval Haldia can remember dropping his parents Pavan Haldia and Kavita Haldia off at the airport for their trip to Kathmandu, spending a few days sightseeing before moving on to Mount Kailash.He spoke to the BBC from the south London Sanatan Mandir temple, where 16 people from the community have been missing since Wednesday."Everyone here is in the same position and that's really helping," he told the BBC. "I'm just trying to stay positive, no news is good news sometimes, I guess.""Obviously it's a very difficult time. There's ups and downs when you think about certain things, but we're just hoping and really praying that everything's ok and they are going to be back soon," he says.Elsewhere, Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, from Slough, was among 27 travellers linked to the tour company who remain unaccounted for.Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told The Times: "I know that she's in Nepal for sure, so even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there."University of Kent graduate Nabhi Das from Streatham in South London has also been widely reported as missing Nepal.A British psychiatrist is also among the missing.Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims in Tibet when the floods hit, the Telegraph reports.His wife, Manjula Atmakur, has travelled to Nepal to help look for him.She said she felt let down by the British government's response to the flooding.Several of those missing had been making a pilgrimage to the sacred Hindu site of Mount Kailash, Nepalese tour operator The Trekkers' Society said.The operator said nine British nationals on one of its tours to the site were among those unaccounted for, including four males, aged 14, 50, 50 and 54, and five females, aged 40, 46, 50, 50 and 53.Tour companies including Alpine Eco Trek, The Trekkers' Society, Himalayan Glacier US, Kailash Journeys and Fishtail Tours have reported missing British nationals while on trips with the companies.Alpine Eco Trek said it has not been able to establish contact with 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash and were in the region when the flash floods struck.

schema.headline: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal

title: How Victorian Eastbourne realised it needed public loos
description: How a seaside town realised it needed public loosImage source, Kevin GordonImage caption, The Queens Hotel, boasting 60 rooms, was one of the faciliti
body: How a seaside town realised it needed public loosImage source, Kevin GordonImage caption, The Queens Hotel, boasting 60 rooms, was one of the facilities without a toiletBySimon FurberReporting fromin Eastbourne and Cash MurphySouth EastEastbourne has a fascinating history with one of life's most basic amenities: the toilet.In the Victorian era, as the town grew from a small settlement into one of Britain's most fashionable seaside resorts, thousands of tourists arrived by train each year.But the number of toilets did not match the number of visitors and a popular boat race in 1870 laid bare the lack of facilities."It's said that over 1,000 people used a small stable near the pier to go the toilet," historian Kevin Gordon told Secret Sussex.Figure caption, Eastbourne's battle with convenience"I'm not even sure if it was plumbed in; this obviously made the council realise that they needed to do something about this problem," Gordon explained. He said that one of the first toilets was built at the Wish Tower slopes close to the seafront, on land that was then owned by the military.While that toilet, which was notably only for men, was put in place in 1873, the first sign for it was not erected until 17 years later.A growing interest in building public toilets put Trinity Trees - a street in the centre of Eastbourne that eventually became another site for an early public toilet - at the centre of a debate. Plans to construct facilities were not universally embraced."[Some] people didn't want a toilet there at all. The Duke of Devonshire said he didn't want any toilets, public toilets, on his land because he called them 'violations of public decency'," said Gordon. Image source, Kevin GordonImage caption, Gentleman's toilets were hidden in the bushes near the Wish Tower, pictured in the late 1800sEven when toilets were built, they weren't for everyone. Gordon said the council didn't introduce the first public ladies' toilets until 1900. Plans had previously been turned down by the council, which remember, was male led, he said. According to Gordon, the town's soaring popularity prompted the council to finally take action.He said: "Thousands of people were coming down here by train, and I don't think the council initially realised that they needed the ordinary things that we all want."The refurbished toilets at Eastbourne Pier, the bandstand, Holywell and Beachy Head are now £1 to use.Secret SussexExplore more fascinating stories from SussexListen and subscribe for the latest episode of Secret Sussex

title: At least 37 dead and hundreds evacuated after strike on Kyiv weapons depot
description: Thirty-seven people have died and almost 400 have been evacuated after a Russian drone strike hit a depot storing weapons for Ukraine's military near
body: Thirty-seven people have died and almost 400 have been evacuated after a Russian drone strike hit a depot storing weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area on the outskirts of Kyiv.The strike caused shells, mines and drones to detonate late on Friday, triggering a blast that damaged nearby properties including a care home for the elderly and disabled, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.He said the storage site "definitely shouldn't have been there" and that an investigation had been launched into "terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosive right next to people".The attack is the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv in recent months, prompting renewed anger.Four children are among the 42 people injured in Friday night's explosion, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko, with a rescue operation ongoing at the site, in the Bucha district, on Saturday.Russia's Ministry of Defence said in a statement that its forces had targeted "an ammunition depot" in Myla, a village to the west of the Ukrainian capital, holding "components and launch boosters for FP-1/FP-2 long-range unmanned aerial vehicles".The explosion damaged about 130 homes in the village."Everything is completely damaged," local resident Liubov Pavlenko, 45, told the BBC while inspecting her home around 200m from the ammunition warehouse."There are cracks all around the entire perimeter, and cracks around the windows. Basically, the structural integrity has been compromised," she added."I'm still kind of numb. I don't know… once I come around a little tomorrow, I'll probably have an even bigger breakdown."Zelensky said the decision to store explosives in the village was "absolutely unacceptable", adding: "Criminal proceedings have been opened on charges of official negligence."The office of Ukraine's prosecutor general earlier said it was reviewing the "legality of the placement and storage of explosive objects and materials" near residential buildings in Myla.It said the "actions of officials who made the relevant decisions" would also be investigated.However, Zelensky earlier stated that "there are regulations in place - ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas", adding "appropriate conclusions will certainly be drawn". He referenced the strike on an ammunition warehouse in Vyshneve in July, which caused a secondary detonation that killed nine, injured dozens more and damaged more than 280 homes.Friday night's explosion has raised fresh questions about why munitions were being stored so close to people's homes, especially given the regularity of Russian aerial attacks."The authorities, the Ministry of Defence - why was this allowed at the depots, in a place where there used to be food?" Borys Daniyluk, 61, said."Why were ammunition and weapons stored there, next to a populated village? There are no words, just emotions."Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky expressed regret that a "lesson" had not been learned following the explosion in Vyshneve.The investigation into that incident revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company that had not complied with regulations regarding storage of explosives near residential buildings.Zelensky indicated that the Myla depot had been operated by Ukraine's armed forces."In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence," Koretsky said on Telegram."Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again."Meanwhile, Tkachenko said a 14-year-old was killed in a separate attack in the Boryspil district, while Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said a two-year-old had died after a Russian drone crashed in Obolonskyi.He added that five people, including an 18-year-old girl, were injured in fresh strikes on the capital on Saturday morning. Five people have been killed across the country over the past day, according to local officials.Zelensky reported further overnight strikes in Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia, as the Ukrainian army said it had shot down 233 Russian drones.Russia and Ukraine have been intensifying their aerial attacks in recent months, with Kyiv focusing its operations on Russian economic targets.Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies.

schema.headline: At least 37 dead and hundreds evacuated after strike on Kyiv weapons depot

title: Big Church Festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls
description: Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a man died and six other people were injured by a falling sign.Sussex Police said i
body: Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a man died and six other people were injured by a falling sign.Sussex Police said it had been called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park, near Steyning in West Sussex, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.It was later confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne in East Sussex had died.The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them."And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events. "May the God of comfort and healing be with them all."South East Coast Ambulance service said four of the six people injured were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, with two people having serious injuries.The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.The festival began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident."We are working with the emergency services, police and the Health and Safety Executive as they establish the circumstances surrounding today's incident," the organisers said."We are incredibly grateful to everyone who responded, and to our teams and community for the care they have shown one another."

schema.headline: Big Church Festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls
